title: Keep humans accountable
subtitle: Use the tools. Own the consequences.
description: Check AI-assisted claims, respect information boundaries, and make correction possible. Every scenario and number is fictional.

lessons.title: A draft is not evidence
lessons.objective: Verify AI-assisted claims and preserve accountable human review.
lessons.takeaway: AI can suggest the wording; someone still has to support the claim.
lessons.fieldwork: Review a fictional AI-written pitch. Underline every claim that would need outside evidence before you would send it.

items.title: Check before polishing
items.teach: Fluent wording does not establish accuracy or feasibility. Review consequential claims against reliable evidence and the people responsible for delivery before treating a draft as ready.
items.say: A polished promise still needs a real basis.
items.ethics: Who has verified what the customer may rely on?
items.prompt: An AI draft promises a two-week integration. Your delivery lead estimates four weeks, and the buyer has not yet seen the draft. What is the strongest next step before sending?
options: Replace “two weeks” with “rapid” and send it.
Confirm a feasible scope and revise the promise accordingly.
Keep two weeks because the draft cites industry practice.
why: Vague wording can preserve the same misleading expectation.
This grounds the promise in the team’s actual ability to deliver.
A generic claim does not override the known delivery constraint.

items.title: A claim review routine
items.teach: For a draft that has not been sent, use this review routine: identify consequential claims, check them against evidence and delivery authority, revise unsupported wording, then approve the final version. It is a practical routine, not a universal sequence for every incident.
items.say: Find the claims. Check the basis. Fix the draft. Own the release.
items.ethics: Can the final reviewer explain what supports each important promise?
items.prompt: Put the just-taught routine in order for an unsent proposal.
items.explain: Checking before approval helps prevent others from relying on unsupported claims. A discovered live error may require immediate notification rather than this drafting sequence.

items.title: Make the interaction understandable
items.teach: Transparency should help people understand consequential AI involvement and reach an accountable human. A disclosure is useful when it changes how someone can evaluate, question, or act on the interaction.
items.say: Explain the tool where it affects the person’s choice.
items.ethics: Can the customer tell what the system can decide and how to question it?
items.prompt: A fictional sales chatbot can explain plan features but cannot approve exceptions. Customers keep mistaking its replies for a manager’s binding approval. Which change best addresses that problem?
options: Add a long generic AI notice to an unrelated page.
Tell customers every reply is unofficial even when features are accurate.
Explain its limits and route exceptions to a human.
why: The notice is unlikely to correct the consequential misunderstanding.
A blanket dismissal obscures useful information and still leaves the approval process unclear.
This explains the specific limit and provides a way to obtain an accountable decision.

items.title: The generated shortlist
items.teach: AI-generated assessments can contain unsupported inferences as well as false facts. Check the evidence relevant to the decision rather than treating confidence or ranking as proof.
items.say: An AI ranking is a proposal to inspect.
items.ethics: Is an unverified inference deciding who gets an opportunity?
items.prompt: A fictional vendor-selection assistant ranks a small supplier last for “likely unreliability,” but gives no supporting evidence. The committee wants a defensible shortlist. What should it do?
options: Check delivery evidence against consistent criteria.
Accept the ranking because the explanation sounds confident.
Move the supplier to first place to offset the possible error.
why: This tests the consequential inference without assuming the supplier is reliable or unreliable.
Confidence is not evidence for the assessment.
Reversing an unsupported ranking without investigation creates another unsupported judgment.

lessons.title: Personal without intrusive
lessons.objective: Use relevant information for an understood purpose without exploiting sensitive inferences.
lessons.takeaway: Useful personalization follows a real need, not a private vulnerability.
lessons.fieldwork: Write two fictional outreach lines: one based on a stated business need and one based on an intrusive inference. Explain why you would send only the first.

items.title: Available is not appropriate
items.teach: Information being visible does not settle whether it is appropriate to use for a new purpose. Consider relevance, the person’s expectations, sensitivity, and possible harm before personalizing a pitch.
items.say: Access to a fact is not a reason to exploit it.
items.ethics: Does this detail help the request or target a vulnerability?
items.prompt: A prospect publicly asked for accessible booking software. An AI tool also infers a family health crisis from unrelated posts. To tailor a respectful business message, what should you use?
options: The health inference, framed as sympathy.
The stated booking requirement, without the health inference.
Both details, because both came from public material.
why: The inference is sensitive, uncertain, and unnecessary to the business request.
The stated requirement is relevant to the person’s expressed need.
Public availability does not remove the sensitivity or purpose mismatch.

items.title: Needed for this request?
items.teach: Collecting only relevant information reduces unnecessary exposure and focuses the conversation. A field being interesting to a seller does not make it needed for the customer’s stated request.
items.say: Ask for what the task needs.
items.ethics: Could the same request be handled without this detail?
items.prompt: A fictional buyer requests a delivery quote for office furniture. Classify the details for calculating delivery cost; no other service is being requested.

entries.why: Distance and timing affect this delivery estimate.

entries.text: Access details such as stairs or a freight lift
entries.why: These affect the work and equipment needed.
It is not needed to calculate this office delivery.
It is unrelated to the requested quote.

items.explain: This is a purpose-specific judgment. Information relevant to a different service would need its own justification.

items.title: A new audience is a new decision
items.teach: Information shared for one conversation should not casually become a lead for another organization. Check the intended purpose and obtain appropriate permission before making a new disclosure.
items.say: An introduction should not surprise the person being introduced.
items.ethics: Did they agree to this information reaching this audience?
items.prompt: A buyer gives you an email address to receive your quote. A partner asks for it to pitch a separate service, and the buyer has not agreed to that. What best preserves the buyer’s control?
options: Forward it and let them unsubscribe if uninterested.
Add the buyer to the partner’s contact list, asking the partner not to call yet.
Ask whether they want the specific introduction before sharing.
why: The buyer is exposed to a new use before having a choice about it.
Delaying the call does not undo the disclosure: the partner already has the address for a purpose the buyer did not accept.
This lets the buyer decide about the new purpose and audience.

items.title: The helpful introduction
items.teach: A person can welcome help without agreeing to every possible disclosure. Define what would be shared, with whom, and for what purpose before acting on their behalf.
items.say: Make the proposed help specific enough to accept or decline.
items.ethics: What exactly is the person agreeing to share?
items.prompt: A fictional workshop participant mentions a transport difficulty. You know a volunteer coordinator who may help, but the participant has not asked you to share their details. What should happen first?
options: Ask permission for a specific, limited introduction.
Send the coordinator the participant’s full message immediately.
Assume privacy means you cannot mention the possible help.
why: The participant can choose whether the help and disclosure suit them.
The full message may reveal more than needed, without agreement.
You can describe an option without sharing the person’s information.

lessons.title: Build a route to correction
lessons.objective: Connect incentives, decision ownership, and repair rather than relying on individual good intentions.
lessons.takeaway: Accountability needs an owner, a route to raise concerns, and a way to correct the result.
lessons.fieldwork: For a fictional promise, write who owns delivery, who can authorize a change, and how the buyer can report a problem.

items.title: What the dashboard rewards
items.teach: Metrics can make some actions easier to justify and others harder to pursue. Evaluate what a target encourages and whether complaints, fit, and delivery failures can still influence decisions.
items.say: A target teaches people what the organization will notice.
items.ethics: Which harms disappear if this is the only number watched?
items.prompt: A fictional team rewards signed contracts only. Agents are discouraged from recording poor-fit customers, and avoidable cancellations are rising. Which change most directly addresses that incentive problem?
options: Tell agents to care more while leaving the process unchanged.
Track fit and delivery; let staff report concerns.
Stop collecting any performance information.
why: Good intentions alone do not change the incentive or reporting barrier.
This makes the neglected outcomes visible and gives staff a concrete way to act.
Removing all information makes it harder to identify improvement or harm.

items.title: Who owns which step?
items.teach: A title alone does not establish authority for every decision. Identify the person who can validate a promise, authorize a remedy, and communicate the agreed action.
items.say: Ownership means knowing who can do what.
items.ethics: Are you promising a remedy you cannot authorize?
items.prompt: In this fictional team, match each explicit responsibility to its owner.
pairs: Checks whether the promised work can be delivered
Approves a refund under the team’s policy
Keeps the customer informed about the agreed next step
items.explain: One person may hold several roles, but the responsibilities still need to be clear. The exercise uses this team’s stated arrangement, not a universal organization chart.

items.title: Raise a concern that can be acted on
items.teach: A useful escalation identifies the claim, the evidence, the affected decision, and the action needed. Organizational barriers are real; a concrete route and accountable recipient make follow-through more possible.
items.say: Make the concern specific enough to resolve.
items.ethics: Will someone with authority receive the facts in time to prevent reliance?
items.prompt: You discover a proposal still promises a feature the delivery lead says is unavailable. Your manager can pause sending, and the proposal has not left the company. Which message is most actionable?
options: “Something about this deal feels off.”
“I disagree with the sales culture in general.”
“This feature is unavailable; please pause this proposal while we correct the scope.”
why: It signals concern but does not identify the issue or needed action.
The broad critique does not resolve the immediate unsupported promise.
It connects a checkable problem to an authorized, timely action.

items.title: An error with a route out
items.teach: Correction requires more than admitting that a system or person made a mistake. Give affected people an understandable account and a practical way to obtain a reviewed decision.
items.say: Make the correction reachable, not merely announced.
items.ethics: Can the affected person get a consequential error reconsidered?
items.prompt: A fictional booking system wrongly labels a customer ineligible for a discount. Staff can review eligibility, but the customer only sees “computer says no.” What change best provides accountability?
options: Explain the relevant rule and offer a staffed review route.
Add “AI may be wrong” beneath the same final rejection.
Automatically give every customer every discount.
why: This makes the basis understandable and allows correction of a specific error.
The warning acknowledges uncertainty without giving the person recourse.
That bypasses the eligibility question instead of creating a review process.
